Obliterate

uh-BLIT-er-ayt -- from Latin ob- ('against, over') + littera ('letter'): literally 'to strike out the letters.' · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To obliterate to destroy something so completely that no trace of it remains; to erase or wipe out utterly.

The renovation crew's sledgehammers obliterated the last standing wall of the old gymnasium within an hour.

Worked Example

Restorers examining the old fresco found that centuries of candle smoke and flaking plaster had left absolutely nothing of the original mural's colors or lines -- not even a faint outline survived.

When something is destroyed so thoroughly that no trace of it remains at all, it has been obliterated -- notice this is about erasing a thing or a mark, not defeating a living opponent (that's annihilate, taught later in this unit).

How Obliterate Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

erase

erase: to rub out or remove completely

expunge

expunge: to erase or remove completely, especially from an official record

Antonyms

preserve

preserve: to keep something safe from harm or loss

safeguard

safeguard: to protect something from harm or damage

How Strong Is It? — erase → obliterate → expunge

erase vs. obliterate

erase vs. obliterate: Erase is a simple, everyday word, often literal -- erasing a pencil mark or a word on a whiteboard. Obliterate is far stronger, used for large-scale, total destruction that leaves nothing behind at all.

expunge vs. obliterate

expunge vs. obliterate: Expunge is close in strength to obliterate, but it's a more formal, narrower word, usually used for official records or written history, while obliterate can describe destroying anything physical or abstract.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — ob-

prefix — ob-: against, over (Latin)

root — -liter-

root — -liter-: letter (Latin (littera))

suffix — -ate

suffix — -ate: to make or do; forms a verb (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Latin ob- ('against, over') plus littera ('letter') plus the verb suffix -ate: literally 'to strike over the letters' until they cannot be read. That is why obliterate means to erase or destroy without a trace.
